diagnostic_evidence.quote: Then Algorithm~\ref{algo_implement:whole} generates a pair $(x^k, y^k)$ in at most $\widehat{K}_\epsilon$ iterations such that $x^k$ is an $(\epsilon, \gamma \epsilon^\sigma/(4L_f))$-stationary point of problem~\eqref{intro_problem}
a point $x$ is called an $(\epsilon, r)$-stationary point of the problem $\min_x \phi(x)$ if $\dist(x, \cS_\epsilon) \leq r$

issues.failure_explanation: The proved guarantee controls distance to a point with residual at most ε, not the residual at the generated point. These are substantively different: for Ψ(x)=|x| and ε<1, a nonzero point within radius r of zero satisfies the defined criterion while its residual is 1. Moreover, when σ<1, the proved localization radius is not O(ε). Thus the displayed rates do not establish the advertised single-parameter O(ε) accuracy.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the accuracy throughout as (ε, γε^σ/(4L_f))-stationarity. An O(ε) residual guarantee requires additional analysis; even obtaining an O(ε) localization radius by reparameterization can worsen the advertised rates when σ<1.
issues.overall_effect: The introductory accuracy promise is stronger than the precise two-parameter guarantees established later.
issues.title: The introductory accuracy claim drops the localization error
issues.why_classification: The source-supported correction changes the central advertised accuracy guarantee to the weaker neighborhood-stationarity guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: It is also well-known that $\partial (\phi_1 + \phi_2)(x) = \nabla \phi_1(x) + \partial \phi_2(x)$ if $\phi_1$ is differentiable and $\phi_2$ is locally Lipschitz continuous at $x$

issues.failure_explanation: Let φ(t)=t² sin(1/t) for t≠0 and φ(0)=0. This function is locally Lipschitz and differentiable at zero, with derivative zero, but its nearby derivatives have limit set [-1,1], so its Clarke subdifferential at zero is [-1,1]. Taking φ₂=0 also disproves the stated sum rule under mere differentiability.

failure_location.quote: When $\phi$ differentiable,  then $\partial \phi$ coincides with the gradient $\nabla \phi$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require continuous differentiability locally, or strict differentiability at the point, in both assertions. The smooth components and the locally Hölder-smooth maximal function used later have the needed stronger regularity.
issues.overall_effect: Two preliminary subdifferential-calculus assertions are false at the stated regularity.
issues.title: Mere differentiability does not collapse the Clarke subdifferential
issues.why_classification: A standard local regularity correction preserves the substantive results and their rates.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We now define an approximate stationary point for the problem $\min_x \phi(x)$, where $\phi$ is a locally Lipschitz continuous function.

issues.failure_explanation: The assumptions allow indicator penalties. For example, p=I_[0,1], q=0 and f(x,y)=-y² satisfy the assumptions, including a global inner KL inequality, but Ψ=I_[0,1] is not locally Lipschitz on an ambient neighborhood of either endpoint. The footnote's extended-valued subdifferential convention does not make Ψ locally Lipschitz.

failure_location.quote: As will be shown later, under mild assumptions, the minimax problem~\eqref{intro_problem} can be viewed as a special case of this problem. Consequently, the following definition applies to problem~\eqref{intro_problem} as well.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Extend the stationarity definition explicitly to proper extended-valued composite objectives using an appropriate extended-valued subdifferential, and remove the claim that Ψ itself is locally Lipschitz.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed reduction to locally Lipschitz minimization and the declared scope of the stationarity definition do not literally include the permitted constrained problems.
issues.title: Allowed constrained objectives are not locally Lipschitz objectives
issues.why_classification: A standard extension of the definition preserves the intended constrained scope, algorithm, and bounds.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In addition, by convention, we set $\partial p(x) = \emptyset$ for any $x \notin \operatorname{dom}\,p$.
We also adopt the convention that $\operatorname{dist}(0, \emptyset) = \infty$.

issues.failure_explanation: Here p is the indicator of [1,2]. Every admissible open Ω contains points x>2 sufficiently close to 2. At those points the stated convention makes the KL threshold infinite, so the assumption requires the global inner KL inequality. But y=π has zero inner stationarity residual and positive gap x(1+√2/2), contradicting that inequality for every C>0. The example's restricted-x level-set calculation does not establish Assumption (iii).

failure_location.quote: For example, the minimax problem in Example~\eqref{example} satisfies the local KL condition but not the global one.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Withdraw the claimed applicability of Assumption (iii) to this example and distinguish its valid restricted-x level-set bound from the stronger open-neighborhood assumption. Retaining the example as a covered application requires changing hypotheses and the boundary analysis.
issues.overall_effect: The framework does not cover its motivating constrained example as claimed.
issues.title: The motivating example does not satisfy the stated local KL assumption
issues.why_classification: This requires a genuine but limited correction of the advertised scope; the conditional formal theory can remain intact.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: x^{k+1} = \mathop{\arg\min}_{x \in \cB(x^k, r)} \Big\{ \langle \nabla_x f(x^{k}, y^{k}), x \rangle + \frac{L_k}{2} \|x - x^k\|^2 + p(x) \Big\}.
the proximal operators of $p$ and $q$ can be computed exactly.

issues.failure_explanation: The update requires the proximal operator of p plus a moving-ball indicator, not the proximal operator of p alone. These operators are not generally reducible to one another by one evaluation; even projecting an ordinary proximal point onto the ball fails for anisotropic quadratic p. A multiplier search or another constrained solver is generally necessary, but neither its construction nor its cost is supplied.

failure_location.quote: We first observe from Algorithm~\ref{algo_implement:whole} that the number of evaluations of the proximal operator $p$ equals the number of iterations.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Explicitly assume an oracle for the ball-constrained proximal subproblem and count those calls instead of ordinary proximal evaluations of p. Alternatively, provide and charge a separate constrained-proximal solver.
issues.overall_effect: The bound of at most K̂_ε ordinary proximal evaluations of p, and the asserted implementation under the stated oracle assumptions, are unsupported.
issues.title: A ball-constrained update is charged as one proximal evaluation of p
issues.why_classification: A contained change of oracle model or an additional subproblem solver is needed, while the outer iteration and gradient-count analysis can remain comparable.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The algorithm is initialized at $(x^0, y^0) = (0, 0)$.
We run the algorithm for 10{,}000 iterations and return the final output denoted by $(x_\epsilon, y_\epsilon)$.

issues.failure_explanation: Every outer step has length at most r. Since F* is L_f-Lipschitz on the feasible ball and the numerical penalty is nonnegative with p(0)=0, after 10,000 steps Ψ(x_ε)≥Ψ(0)-10,000 L_f r=Ψ(0)-25(10^-2)^0.1≈Ψ(0)-15.774. This bound also holds after averaging instances. The first row instead reports a decrease of 225.58, and every other reported actual decrease also violates the bound.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must reconcile the implementation, step radius, and iteration count, and recompute or withdraw the reported numerical values.
issues.overall_effect: The actual-final-value column cannot result from the stated algorithm, parameters, initialization, and iteration count.
issues.title: Reported objective decreases are impossible under the stated step radius
issues.why_classification: Comparable numerical findings cannot be recovered by a justified local edit; the experiment must be reconciled and recomputed or abandoned.

issues.failure_explanation: Closedness of q means lower semicontinuity, not closedness of its effective domain. For example, q(t)=-log t on t>0, extended by +∞ elsewhere, is proper closed convex with nonclosed domain. Thus boundedness of the trajectory does not, by the stated argument, place a cluster point in the finite domain of F.

failure_location.quote: In addition, notice from Assumption \ref{ass:Lip_Smo_KL} that $\dom\,F(x, \cdot)$ is closed.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Take a bounded-trajectory cluster point in the ambient space first. Upper semicontinuity of F and convergence of the trajectory values to the finite value F*(x) then give F(x,y*)≥F*(x), proving both domain membership and optimality without assuming a closed domain.
issues.overall_effect: The cluster-point step in the growth-bound proof is unjustified, leaving its error-bound and smoothness consequences unsupported by that proof.
issues.title: The growth-bound proof incorrectly assumes the inner effective domain is closed
issues.why_classification: A short semicontinuity argument preserves the growth constant and all downstream guarantees.

issues.failure_explanation: The assumptions do not make X=dom p closed. The closed convex function p(t)=-log t on t>0, extended by +∞ elsewhere, is a counterexample to that inference. Consequently the proof cannot infer that the limit lies in X, and hence in Ω, before applying the subsequent subdifferential arguments.

failure_location.quote: It then follows from $x^k \to x$ and the closedness of $\cX$ that $x\in\cX$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Decompose the bounded subgradients s^k into bounded F* subgradients and p subgradients. The latter are then bounded; a convergent subsequence and the closed graph of the convex subdifferential ∂p establish x∈dom p before invoking outer semicontinuity at x.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of openness, which is used to extend differentiability to all nonstationary points, contains an unsupported domain-membership step.
issues.title: The openness proof incorrectly assumes dom p is closed
issues.why_classification: A routine closed-graph argument repairs the proof without adding a closed-domain assumption or weakening any rate.

issues.failure_explanation: No hypothesis guarantees that the set defining K̄_ε is nonempty or has a largest element. It is empty for a run consisting entirely of approximate stationary points; an infinite algorithm is also not shown to have a last nonstationary visit. The set defining K̲_ε can likewise be empty when r is sufficiently large. Nevertheless the lemma and outer proof use these quantities as defined numerical bounds.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Delete the unnecessary K̄_ε restriction and retain the explicit nonstationary-prefix hypothesis already present. Define K̲_ε using the maximum of the displayed set union {0}; the existing decay estimates supply finiteness.
issues.overall_effect: The convergence lemma's hypotheses and the outer proof's comparison with K̄_ε are not well-defined for all permitted cases.
issues.title: The convergence lemma uses maxima that need not exist
issues.why_classification: These local definition changes preserve the convergence argument, iteration bound, and advertised parameter regimes.
